utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today on Tuesday the 6th of March I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and all those who are assisting us in our work. I'll first give the floor to the registrar for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. 4D has submitted a list of objections to documents tendered through Witness Josip Praljak. Such list shall be given Exhibit number IC 472. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we move into private session for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please call the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Mundis, according to our calculations we have another two hours and 51 minutes at our disposal, but as I know you well, I know that you won't be requiring all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I remain optimistic that Your Honour will be proven right in this instance with respect to the time. I don't anticipate that I'll need a full two hours and 51 minutes to complete the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you in advance, Mr. Mundis. Good day, sir. I hope you spent an agreeable evening in The Hague, and we will continue with your testimony today. If you can hear what I am saying, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I can hear you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Biskic. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can return the binder to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while that's being done, yesterday, when we broke, sir, we were talking about -- or we were about to start talking about the second meeting concerning the closing of the collection centres. Do you recall, sir, approximately when that second meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 13th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, if you recall what some of the general topics at that second meeting concerned?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we continued to implement the decree of the president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna on disbanding the collection centres. It was a report of the teams that we had established at the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please turn to the document that's been tabbed 7143. This is P 07143. It's about halfway through the binder, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two documents, 7243. Perhaps there's an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's 7143. It should follow 7194.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You now have that document before you, 7143?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the minutes of a meeting that was held on the 13th of December in Posusje, and it concerns implementing the order of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It was an order on disbanding collection centres. And as I have already said, these are minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a stenographic record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I understand that they're minutes. Do you recall, sir, having had an opportunity to review these minutes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, whether there are any significant errors or omissions in these minutes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember there shouldn't be any errors, but minutes are never completely faithful to what is said as far as the contents and quality of the minutes are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, at the -- at the -- towards the top of the document under the list of persons who were present we see the name of Mr. Vladislav Pogarcic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, if you know the reason why Mr. Pogarcic attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was probably designated on behalf of the office of the president of Herceg-Bosna, because he was the head of the president's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, if you could please turn to page 5 of these minutes. Approximately four or five lines from the bottom of that document, and this is on page 13 of the English translation but at the bottom of page 5 in the Croatian language, there is a reference to a statement made by Mr. Saric. Do you see that? I'm sorry, this is the bottom of page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you read what it says about Mr. Saric and Mr. Jukic? Can you please read that out loud for us?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mr. Saric brought up the problem of the state of the detainees as far as their nourishment is concerned and the state of the sick." And, "Mr. Jukic replied that the prisoners had been receiving treatment to get them into better physical condition for three weeks and that they were receiving food regularly and that their living conditions had been improved."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, perhaps it's a translation error, but in the original document is there also a reference with respect to what Mr. Saric said about the media and the media presence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read Mr. Saric's words out, and he does mention media presence or monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection, sir, as to what that conversation concerned with respect to the presence of the media and this issue that you've just read out?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably Mr. Saric meant that the media would be present when the collection centres were disbanded and when the detainees were either sent to the BH army side or third countries or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were any discussions about the impact of the media with respect to the collection centres and the disbandment of those collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any discussions, and I think they were present when the collection centres were dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, as a result of the decision to disband the detention centres or the collection centres, did you personally issue any orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the jobs that the military police administration were to do and the security and information service, then certainly I regulated that area through an order of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before we turn to that order, sir, I neglected to ask you, these -- these two meetings that you told us about in December 1993, was Mr. Pusic in attendance at those meetings concerning the disbanding of the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the first meeting he was. I'm just looking at who was there. And I do believe that he attended the second meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know why --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He attend the both meetings. Mr. Berislav Pusic was there both times as the representative of the office for the release of persons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak slower when he comes to titles, headings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, they've asked -- I don't know if you've heard that. The interpreter asked if we could slow down, particularly with respect to titles and headings of different individuals. Let's turn now, sir, to document 7149.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an order to the military police administration and the administration of the SIS and their part in putting into practice the disbanding of the collection centre, and the conclusions from working meetings of the 11th and 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, the first paragraph or the first numbered paragraph of this order makes reference to the Heliodrom prisoner of war shelter, and my question to you, sir, is at this point in time, 13 December 1993, who was the commander of the Heliodrom prisoner of war shelter?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of December the commander of the company for providing security to the shelter of POWs at Heliodrom had and Ljubuski, Mr. Stanko Bozic, and we saw a document yesterday by which I appointed him as the acting person performing these function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you now turn your attention, sir, to paragraph 2 of this document, there's reference to transfer of persons not categorised as prisoners of war to Gabela. Do you know, sir, at this point in time, 13 December 1993, who was responsible or in command of the facility at Gabela?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that it was Mr. Bosko Previsic, and when they started to disband all the collection centres Gabela was a transitory centre and managed as such but I don't know who was responsible at the time. Now, for those who were supposed to go on to third countries or who were supposed to pass to the side under the control of the BH army, then that part of the task was to have been done by the commission for exchanges, the office for displaced persons and refugees cooperating with the international ICRC committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, at the time this document was promulgated, that is the 13th of December, 1993, were persons being detained for whom criminal reports or criminal charges were to be filed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All persons who remained in the POW shelter were treated as prisoners of war or individuals who were incarcerated against whom criminal reports had been filed. They were in detention too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, if there were such persons in the second category, that's persons incarcerated against whom criminal reports had not been filed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I hate to interrupt but I believe the previous answer was not properly translated. Again, if the gentleman could be asked the question and be given an opportunity to answer it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask again, sir. On the 13th of December, 1993, were persons being detained for whom criminal reports or criminal charges were to be filed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All persons who remained in the POW shelter Heliodrom had the status of prisoners of war or detainees against whom criminal reports had been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, as of 13 December 1993, approximately how many persons fell into the category of detainees against whom criminal reports had been filed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that earlier on in some of the documents we found that there were about 1.000-odd persons who remained in the POW shelter Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I have a clarification, please? You have now answered that all these prisoners were persons, those who went to Gabela, persons against whom criminal reports had been filed. On the other hand, on the 13th December, in the paper before us under number 5 you give the order to the prosecutor, "... immediately file criminal reports against all detainees." It is difficult to understand this if one assumes that these reports had already been filed before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not mention Gabela. I mentioned the shelter of the POW at Heliodrom or, rather, the detainees who remained in the POW shelter Heliodrom after the detention centres or collection centres had been disbanded, and part of the people who remained in the Heliodrom POW shelter enjoyed the status of prisoners of war, and a portion of those persons were persons against whom criminal reports had been filed, and some of them, criminal charges had not yet been filed but there were grounds for criminal reports to be file. And that is why in point 5 of the same order I issue orders that in cooperation with the SIS administration and the military prosecutor and military court that criminal reports should immediately be filed against all detainees who are in the category of detainees who should remain in the POW shelter Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the gentleman could go just slightly slower, so that -- because every word that you say, sir, is very important to us. So if he could be cautioned just to go slightly slower for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, on the basis of what you have told us, one gains the impression that a certain number of detainees were not the object of any complaints and that they -- and that the criminal files had not been charged yet and that legally speaking they were in some sort of vacuum. So having apprised -- been apprised of this situation, you issued orders that criminal proceedings be taken against them straight away or, rather, criminal reports filed immediately. So that is the situation that you came upon when you took up your duties; right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, could you please turn to Exhibit 7155. It's P 07155. Are you familiar with this document, sir, and, if so, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the document. It is a letter addressed to the Red Cross from -- of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and to the commission for exchange about information about how far the decision has been implemented of the 13th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, do you know if criminal proceedings were instituted against any of the 1.119 persons that are referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that criminal reports were filed. I don't know whether any criminal proceedings were taken, but I do know that from December 1993 until April 1994 all the persons who were in the POW shelter at Heliodrom through the exchange commission were indeed exchanged for members of the Croatian Defence Council and Croatian civilians who were held by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Mundis. I would need some clarification here too. It says in this document 1.119 captives is enclosed, a list of captives for whom criminal reports were filed so they are treated as prisoners of war. I do not quite understand the logic of this link, because one would expect prisoners who are charged to be treated as prisoners detained on remand in the context of criminal proceedings, and their status is not at all the same as that of prisoners of war. So could you please explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you -- it says here prisoner -- war detainee and not prisoner of war. A detainee can be anybody who under wartime conditions acted against the state or the system and organisation and institution in control of the area. So that POWs are not mentioned here. It is war detainees that are mentioned, not prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my colleague asked you a question which has preoccupied the Judges, and the Judges have to distinguish between prisoners of war and those people who do not have the status of prisoners of war but who are -- against whom criminal reports have been filed. In a word, when the HVO captures BH army soldiers, for instance, then the BH army soldiers are prisoners of war. When the HVO captures civilians, those civilians can be detained on remand under the condition that there are criminal proceedings against them, which would motivate their incarceration. So do you distinguish in legal terms this distinction that the Judges have to make and which you, too, have to make with respect to the fate of the people who are detained? So did you distinguish between these two categories, prisoners of war and captives who would ultimately be legally prosecuted for some acts that they had perpetrated? And what my colleague has said, that there seems to be a confusion over these two terms and this -- these two types of status. Mr. Karnavas, just a minute. Witness, may I have your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you remember yesterday we discussed this, and I assume you know that part of the Muslim ethnic group or nationality were within the Croatian Defence Council at the beginning the war that started on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Once a conflict broke out between the Muslim armed forces or the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council, then part of those members of the HVO who were Muslims launched an uprising. They were disarmed and incarcerated and criminal reports filed against them, and they were treated as war detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Judge Trechsel, if I may be of some assistance. The gentleman indicated earlier, and my colleague here confirms this, that the document has been mistranslated, and I think that perhaps we could ask the gentleman to read the first sentence, because at least the way my colleague, who is a native speaker, looks at it, it says "war detainee." It doesn't say war prisoner. It talks about detainees. And again, if we go back to the gentleman's testimony from yesterday, it was very, very clear about the distinctions and the categorisations. So I think that for some reason there is a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is correct, and the English translation has made this quite clear. However, the problem is that there is no such legal category as war detainees. It is not a technical term, and therefore it is, with due respect, without any use for the Chamber. For the Chamber, legal categories must be given. And for authorities detaining, they must detain under a title which exists, and there is no such title as war detainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean we can quibble over -- you know, a rose by any other name is a rose. I think we can agree on that. But he does make the distinction between somebody being a prisoner of war versus somebody who has been detained because they're either within -- their own army has misbehaved and that is the distinction the gentleman is making. But I'll leave it to -- you know, we'll argue that at some other point. But I'm not here to defend the gentleman or to defend the terminology that was used at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have given us an explanation and clarified the matter, and you said that amongst the prisoners there were those who were Muslims who had been in the HVO and deserted and were captured and against whom criminal reports had been filed for desertion or some other legal transgression. So is that how we are to understand the distinction that you made between one category and the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, we're making things clearer, thanks to the Judges' questions, largely. Now, my last question. They are prisoners of war, BH army soldiers who have been captured. Then you have old prisoners who were HVO soldiers, Muslims, who deserted. And then there's another category that we encountered, that is to say civilians who were not BH army soldiers at all, neither were they former HVO soldiers. Now, from your point of view, why were those civilians detained? If you can answer that, if you're in a position to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, during the period when the collection centres were being disbanded, do you recall whether or not you received reports from Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we received reports, most of us did, who took part in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of these reports from Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of those reports was to inform us about how many people who had been incarcerated had left, whether they went to the BH army side or third countries or the HR HB, and also the number who remained in Heliodrom, because in the service for the exchange exact figures were kept, facts and figures about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you turn, please, to document P 07187, or, in your binder, 7187, please. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document relates to, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report by the service for the exchange of detainees and other persons of HR HB of the 15th of December, 1993, and it addresses the implementation of the decision to disband the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to the next document, that is 7246, P 07 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Before we go on to the next document, Witness, can we go back to this document, 07187. Now, look at the second paragraph. The first paragraph says that prisoners of war should be transferred immediately to Heliodrom. Now, the second paragraph seems to me to be interesting as well for us to be able to understand what was going on. It appears to indicate that persons should be transferred who were not characterised as prisoners of war to Gabela so that they could be taken over by the commission for exchange. Now, what did you want to say by that? What does that second paragraph mean?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not a report by me. It is a report by the office for the exchange of persons and other people of the HR HB, and all I can do is to interpret what it says here. Now, if we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Witness. There is definitely a misunderstanding somewhere, because in our files document P 07178, which was called by the Prosecution, is an order signed by Mr. Biskic, and it appears that you have a different document under the same number. So we must be sure that we talk about the same document, otherwise we lose time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have a report that is from Mr. Pusic, but it's 7187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, we have the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there must be some sort of a mix-up. It's 7187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, in the document 07187 we have an order signed by the witness, that is 02-4193. The date is the 13th of December, 1993. And looking at the document in the B/C/S, it's another document which is signed by Stanko Bozic. Has there been a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There would appear to be a mistake. I believe the document that you have, the English translation of the document 7187 is in fact 7149. The English version of 7187 in fact is not a document that the question that Your Honours have asked relates to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you a question about a document, so what document would you like the witness to address and answer questions about, because I don't want to be studying a document that you're not going to deal with. So your question, Mr. Mundis, which document did it apply to, 07149 or the other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, 07187. It appears as though the document in English is available in e-court. Clearly the document the witness referred to in answering my question, he was in fact looking at the correct document that I wanted him to -- to answer questions about. The English version now appears in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To make the confusion complete, let me just draw your attention to the fact that the B/C/S document we have under number 7178 corresponds neither to the English document nor to that which is now on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I apologise for the confusion caused by this document. Unfortunately the version -- or, rather, fortunately in the case of the witness and myself our versions appear to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't say this to blame anybody, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It's possible Your Honour may be looking at the wrong document, if you said 7178. I think the number Mr. Mundis is referring to is 7187. Perhaps Your Honour has -- is that a further mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's a further mistake. On the front of the tab it's 7187; on the back of the tab it's 7178.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But at any rate, Witness, the document that you have before you on which the English is available on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Mundis, I'll withdraw my question and give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, Mr. Biskic, if we could return to this document, 7187, that you have before you. Again, sir, can you tell us what the purpose of this report from Mr. Pusic --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this report was to inform the person how far the decision of the president of the HR HB to disband the collection centres has gone and to see how many detainees had gone where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that is in the period of, say, from the 11th of December until the end of that month, the end of December 1993, do you recall approximately how many reports were received from Mr. Pusic on this subject of detainee or prisoner releases?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what the number was, how many reports, but I think there were four or five at the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to document 7246, that's P 07246. Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a continuation of the report that was sent out for the commission for the exchange of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you, sir, if you could look to the total number of detained persons towards the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, your reaction when you first saw this document with respect to 4.320 detained persons?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember my reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on the approximate proportion of the number of prisoners of war to the overall total number of detained persons?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how many remained and how many were released? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, it would appear that there were 1.089 prisoners of war out of a total of 4.320 detained persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any comments or -- concerning those overall numbers? Does it --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't claim that there weren't some who might have remained in the collection centre for POWs among the others, but I believe the teams that were -- worked because it was the information security service, the military police, and the military prosecutor's office, the military court, and I think there was also a representative of the health service. They composed the teams, and I believe that they conscientiously carried out their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, what the number 700 next to the "Remained to be processed" column refers to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that they were still being processed. That means that those waiting to go to third countries were concerned or those waiting to cross over to the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to help the Judges understand this chart, I would like you to confirm something for us. We have noted that there were 3.620 prisoners. 1.557 were on the Muslim side because it says -- so there's 1.557 who should have been exchanged, because on the ABiH side there was an office for the exchange of prisoners too. So there were 1.557 of them who went to areas under ABiH control. 556 remained in areas under HVO control; 617 went abroad, to Croatia, Germany, France, et cetera; and apparently 1.089 who had to stay there provisionally because they were POWs. Is this how we should understand this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the 700 referred to should be added to the 3.620, or they are part of the 3.620? So should we add this number to the 3.620 or not, because it's not very clear when it comes to these 700 individuals. Should the number 700 be added to 3.620?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, when we have a look at this report it seems that there is a total of 4.320. Those who -- that was the number of POWs. All I can note is what is stated here. They hadn't been processed -- or, rather, they were waiting for visas in order to go to third countries. I assume that that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the 700, shouldn't they be added to the number 1.089, because you said they should be POWs. So should this number be added to 1.089 in order to reach the total of 4.320 that is stated here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the number 1.089 concerns those who remained in the collection centre for POWs. There was 700 in Gabela, and they were waiting to be processed -- or, rather, to go to third countries. So they are not included in the category of those who remained in the collection centre after the collection centres were disbanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So 700, in your opinion. Where were they, in the Heliodrom, in Gabela, Livno, Ljubuski? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of December they were in Gabela, in the Gabela transit centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine. It's a lot clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you turn please to the next document, 7494, P 07494. Sir, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a report from the service for the exchange of prisoners and others. It was addressed to me as the assistant to the minister, and in this letter a suggestion is made according to which some of the detainees in Heliodrom collection centre should be transferred to Gabela because the Heliodrom had too many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on the reference to the transfer to the military investigation prison, VIZ Gabela, which is registered as a military prison?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was registered as such at the time. On the 6th of January, Gabela was no longer functioning in any way. It's a fact that in Heliodrom collection centre for POWs there was not sufficient space. However, I believed that there were exchanges that were being carried out, and I did not provide a positive reply to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, on the Croatian language version of this document there's some handwriting at the bottom. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this says? Can you read the handwriting that's written on this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says on the 9th of January there was my reply that was sent to the military police by fax, and the service for the exchange of prisoners or detainees, and what I wrote down is that I do not agree with this suggestion, and in future everything that concerns prisoners of war should be forwarded to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the very last line, sir, I believe there was another translation error in the English. What does the very last line of that handwriting say?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last line before my signature it says, "In the future, everything should be forwarded to the military police administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the final line which you've indicated is your signature, what does that say?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Colonel Biskic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so that we're all clear, the English says, "Colonel Blaskic." Did you write Colonel Blaskic's name at -- anywhere on this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again as a matter of clarity, you told us that you wrote, "I do not agree" in the handwriting on the bottom of this document. Can you tell us what did you not agree with in this document that was produced by Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not agree with the idea that some of the detainees in the Heliodrom should be transferred to Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you disagree with that idea?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because we had decided where they would be detain. We had established a company to provide security for the POW collection centre, and I believed that the situation should have been maintained as such and that they should be exchanged from that base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I'm going to now return in a little bit more detail to a subject we touched upon yesterday, which was the notion of detainees being taken out for labour. Let me start by asking you, sir, based upon your experience as a military police expert and authority, what is your understanding as to the use of detainees or prisoners of war for purposes of labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the Geneva Conventions, POWs can be used to carry out labour; it depends on their ranks though. And this can be done outside combat areas and within the fields of industry, agriculture, et cetera. That is what is stated in the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any types of labour that prisoners of war could not be engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was information and rumours according to which POWs had been taken to carry out work in areas of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your understanding, sir, based upon the Geneva Conventions as to the legality of such labour by prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously this wasn't in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I believe you told us this yesterday, but at the time of your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina on or about the 8th of November, 1993, do you know if persons who were in the collection centres or prisoner of war centres were being used to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I received such information. I haven't got any specific documents that demonstrate that someone engaged someone else at the front line, but according to reports from the security and information service while -- I received information according to which some POWs had fled from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you received this information about these POWs who had fled from the front line?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was during the preparatory stage for an operation in the Uskoplje sector. It was the first half of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The first half of November, interpreter's correction, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time of your arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina, sir, were you aware of any orders governing the use of prisoner or detainees for labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I hadn't seen any such orders. I said I hadn't been assigned my duties from anyone. I said that I assumed that there were such cases and that was confirmed. Last time you showed me a document which I think was drafted in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember who had signed the document that you just referred to from October 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Milivoj Petkovic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to document 5873? That's P 05873. Mr. Biskic, is this the document you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the third sentence or the third numbered point in this order, were you aware of any prosecutions for failing to comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information, and I wasn't the person within the chain of command who would receive information on the implementation of measures taken by the Main Staff and by commanders at their respective levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, as someone who had some responsibility with respect to military police matters seeing any reports or investigations concerning prosecutions for failure or investigations concerning failure to comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I have already said that there was the criminal military police -- or the crime military police. They did their work, and they acted in accordance with all the information they had at their disposal, but I have no particular information that I could provide you with that I could refer to. But we should make a distinction between command responsibility in this case. Any commander can take disciplinary measures; he has that right. And then there is this order issued by General Milivoj Petkovic, which means that at lower command levels whoever acts in this way will be held to account, will be held responsible. This is not just the work and the duties of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We touched upon this briefly yesterday, sir, but once you became aware of this issue of prisoners and labour, what steps did you take concerning this issue?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggested to the chief of the Main Staff, General Roso, that he should issue an order on prohibiting detainees from collection centres from being taken to carry out work of any kind. And the order should specify precisely who could authorise taking detainees out to work. General Roso issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around the second half of November 1993. In the same order he ordered that all the detainees should be returned to the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please turn to document 7471. That's P 07471. Are you familiar, sir, with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document relates to, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is entitled "Prisoners of war." It concerns a letter of mine that I sent to the ministry -- to the minister of defence, Mr. Perica Jukic; and to the chief of the Main Staff, General Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I draw your attention to the fourth paragraph of this document. There appears to be a reference to two orders in the fourth paragraph, and I'm wondering, sir, if you recall and can comment upon what those orders refer to.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think these orders were issued by the chief of the Main Staff, and they concern the ban on taking detainees out to carry out labour. And it also concerns returning these detainees. I can't really say what the order of the 30th of November referred to and the other order, but it concerned respect for international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the paragraph immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I have a question that I'd like to put to you in reference to this document. You sent this letter to the minister of defence, Mr. Perica Jukic; and to Mr. Ante Roso, personally. What I find hard to understand with regard to your role of assistant -- or, rather, deputy minister responsible for security is the following: Did you occupy a political post, as is the case for a minister, or did you have an administrative role to play? Could you tell me whether you were someone who occupied a political position or administrative position given that you're the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be a deputy minister is usually a political role, but in this case I did not act in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have answered part of my question, a significant part of my question. You said that a deputy minister has a political role to play. As far as Mr. Perica Jukic is concerned, did you have meetings of a political nature with him, meetings that were held to assess the situation, find solutions sometimes of a political kind to military issues and other issues? You have -- you sent this letter to him that concerned POWs, which is an extremely delicate issue. Did you speak to Mr. Jukic about this problem and about the consequences in international terms in -- with regard to the UN, with regard to other consequences, because you know that at the time this Tribunal you are testifying before was established, did you have any discussion was Mr. Jukic that concerned this problem, or is there just this document that outlines the issues relating to POWs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday I said that this is not the only document in which reference is made to POWs. I wasn't acting in my capacity as a politician, and I wasn't assessing what the political consequences of these events would be. I was working as an operations officer, and I was carrying out the tasks that I was responsible for at the time as the deputy minister, but I was absolutely against any violations of the Geneva Conventions and of international humanitarian law. And as of November, to the with all those who occupied certain posts in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna at the time, we dealt with the problems of collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the blockades that you recorded, who was responsible for them? Because you, as the number two person to deal with this issue, since the number one person was Minister Jukic, well, in your opinion where did these obstacles, these difficulties, come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yesterday I said that I encountered no obstacles when carrying out my tasks. Naturally, it's easier to carry out some tasks, and for other tasks you require more time in order to deal with the task at the command level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document we can see that you have mentioned the fact that Major General Matic gave the Mostar defence permission to take 40 prisoners of war, and you say this violated international law and orders, and you wrote, but you didn't ask Mr. Jukic to immediately arrest General Matic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember this letter, it was compiled after my return because I was in Zagreb over the New Year, and from my office I was informed that agreement was given by General Matic that 40 detainees should be given over to the defence of Mostar. That does not mean that they would be at the front line. But I considered that this was something that should not be granted permission for, and it was not authorised. General Matic was under General Roso's responsibility, and my responsibilities were not such that I was able to propose to a minister of defence or the chief of the Main Staff to give them instructions to undertake any measures because a crime had not been committed here. Perhaps the intention was a good one and perhaps those prisoners of war might have been engaged in some sort of work which is allowed by the -- and under the Geneva Conventions, because in the town of Mostar itself the front line was somewhere in the centre of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Biskic, if you allow for this possibility, why did you, I say in quotation, "blindly stop this," and not try to find out whether these prisoners were to be taken to innocent work or to forbidden work? It looks as though you assumed they were used for unlawful work, if one reads your order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me to remember now what I was thinking in 1994 when I wrote this document, but at any rate, I did not agree with the permission granted and I stopped it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, if you could please look at the fifth paragraph of this document, P 07471. There's reference to increasingly frequent requests for work on the front lines, and I'm wondering, sir, what -- if you recall what you based that statement in this document of yours upon.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably my employees from the office were informed that there were requests made of this kind. I didn't see anything in writing. Had I done that, then I would have mentioned that in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's also reference, sir, in that paragraph to the fact that you had not given any such permission for persons to be taken to the front lines for labour. My question is, do you recall on how many occasions you personally gave such permission for persons to be taken to the front lines to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was once, but not up to the front line. What I did was give permission to engage 20 or 30 detainees in the Aluminijum combine in Mostar. And I think that that was in keeping with the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, can you comment upon compliance with the order to return detainees that was issued concerning persons who were taken out to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were problems in returning them. Unfortunately, the order from the chief of the Main Staff issued at the beginning of November and -- or end of November and start of December, it was not respected. So in January once again I think it was the minister of defence, Mr. Jukic, who issued that order. And the last order that was issued in that area was in April 1994, once again from the minister, but at the time it was Mr. Vladimir Soljic. So there were problems in implementing that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know there were problems implementing that order?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the International Committee of the Red Cross through its letters cautioned us and said that some detainees were taken to collection centres. They were taken out and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether you also received some reports from any of the persons under your authority concerning this issue?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Superior to me or subordinate to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Subordinate to you.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether you saw any reports from any of your subordinates on the issue of failure to comply with the order to return detainees who had been taken out for purposes of labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, subordinate to me were the chief of the administration of the military police and the chief of the SIS administration. Now, the chief of the administration of the military police informed me about the problems about returning POWs to the POW shelter. But those who had been -- who were taken out had been returned, but he -- it made no information of somebody from the military police units being taken out and not returned but from other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, to turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. You spoke of your superiors and your subordinates. What I'm interested in is in your superiors. The minister, Minister Jukic, he was above you; right? Now, above the defence minister was the Prime Minister, who at the time was Mr. Prlic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. I object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's an incorrect reading of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sit down. The question can be sensitive. I want to identify the gentleman's superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not sensitive. It's an incorrect reading of the laws, Mr. President. It's an incorrect reading of the statute. That's what I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sit down. Witness, your superiors in this government, who were your superiors, can you tell me? Who was above you successively to the top, from you upwards? You spoke about your subordinates. I understand that, but what I'm interested in is your superiors. So who was your immediate superior and right up to the top? So can you tell us who your superiors were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said but I will repeat the minister of the defence of the HR HB was superior to me and that was Mr. Perica Jukic up until the 25th of February 1994, and after the 25th of February up until my return to Croatia on the 6th of May, 1994, it was the minister, Vladimir Soljic. That was the only person that I reported to. I was only subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. A moment ago you said that you had a political post within the Ministry of Defence. Now, above the minister of defence, to the best of knowledge, was there somebody above the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not say that my post was a political one. I said that mostly in ministries in peacetime and wartime they were political duties and of course power and authority goes to the party that won the elections. I was not a politician myself. Perhaps following on from that logics, the Prime Minister appointed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, you were appointed by the Prime Minister. Who was the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time it was Mr. Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who appointed the defence minister? Who was the defence minister appointed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Was there at the level of the HVO a Supreme Commander? Concerning the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Commander of the Croatian Defence Council was the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The late Boban, Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To summarise what you've just said, the Supreme Commander was Mate Boban. The Prime Minister was Mr. Prlic. The minister of defence was Mr. Jukic, at least on the 4th of January, and you yourself were the assistant to the defence minister; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps now would be the appropriate time for the break, the first scheduled break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give you the floor, I'd just like to tell Mr. Karnavas that I consider it impermissible for counsel to control Judges' questions. That is absolutely impermissible. I asked a question on the structure of government, and the witness answered the about structure, so I don't see where the problem is. And your intervention was a type of pressure exerted upon the Judge, and that is what I wanted to say to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, with the utmost respect, Mr. President, and I do have a lot of respect for all of you. First, the question was rather leading in nature, but number two, there were facts in the question that were -- you were assuming a facts that have not been in evidence or it was a misrepresentation of what is in the statute itself. We're going to clear this up on cross-examination, but I dare say I'm entitled to object for the record purposes as opposed to waiting later on, because I could see very clearly, Mr. President, you're trying to establish, you know, the line -- who is at the top and who is at the bottom in the command and control, and I dare say when we go through the statute, because the Prosecution hasn't done that, they haven't gone through the laws, but I would say that I'm entitled to formally object to the form of the question if it assumes a fact which is not in evidence or which is incorrect with the statute -- with the statute or the laws that are being introduced in this court. And I meant no disrespect, did you I do need to make an objection. And again, I have the utmost respect for you, but there are going to be times where we're all going to disagree, and I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incident is closed. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please now turn to document 7153 in the binder. This is P 07153. Sir, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the subject matter of this report is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report by Mr. Stanko Bozic, the warden of the -- or, rather, the commander of the company for providing security for detainees, to Mr. Radoslav Lavric, acting military police chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the subject of the report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject of the report is lack of compliance with the order to return detainees from doing labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Biskic, whether any follow-up action was taken as a result of this report of Mr. Stanko Bozic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my level steps were taken. The minister was informed again, and the chief of the Main Staff that the order by the chief of the Main Staff was not respected. And for this lack of compliance, the chief of the Main Staff -- it is up to the chief of the Main Staff to take measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you now turn, sir, to document 7021, P 07021. And again, Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what this document concerns?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document also deals with taking out detainees from the collection centre to perform labour by the sector for the defence of Mostar, and it is about the wounding, escape, and death of a detainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Biskic, what steps, if any, were taken as a result of this report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Steps were taken. As I've already said, everything was linked to the implementation of the order from the chief of the Main Staff about the return of detainees or prisoners, and the sector it of the town's defence was under the command of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, sir, when you indicate steps were taken. What types of steps?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Steps were taken whereby the order was repeated several times from the level of the minister of defence with respect to the return prisoners, detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have a report here written on the 3rd of December from Mr. Bozic, and you appointed him, and the report indicates that there were two persons who were killed, one person who was wounded, and two persons who had escaped, and he is telling you that he had no written report about that. When you read this type of report, at your level what are you supposed to do having read a report like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I read a report like this in the post I occupied that means I must make measures to prevent incidents that have kind from happening again. Secondly, as the document was also addressed to Mr. Lavric as the deputy chief of the military police, it automatically implies that on the basis of this document information should be gathered pursuant to these incidents and that the information gathered should be processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you as the number one man, the number one responsible person, because Mr. Lavric was a subordinate of yours, did you not have the task of following up on this incident which was reported to you because the report was addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not say that that was not my job. The fact is that insistence was made upon the people's return, and this is one of the results of the order from the chief of the Main Staff to have the persons returned. And once they were returned, it was establish that certain individuals were wounded. Some had escaped, and some were killed. So on the basis of this information, it is the duty of the crime prevention military police to unleash the process of processing and to uncover the perpetrators linked to this event. I cannot remember at this point in time what the result of all that was, of those steps taken were, but I do believe that in the records of the military police you will find the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw that there was a document from General Petkovic which was quite unambiguous and absolutely forbid this kind of work performed outside. Now, apparently General Petkovic's orders were violated. So within the military system there must be investigations carried out and sanctions taken. So my question is: Were any sanctions taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question right now because I can't remember what happened. All I do know is that I insisted upon the return of these people, and finally sometime in April 1994, I issued an order myself saying that criminal investigations should be carried out against all those perpetrators who violated the Geneva Conventions or in any way infringed upon the rights of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have -- I have two questions, the first just to avoid possible misunderstanding. In this report it says, it's at the bottom of the first page in English: "A group of detainees was returned ... but the others remain there." "The others" does not sort of cynically refer to the two who had been killed but indicates that there were prisoners who continued to be working at the front line for the sector commander. Do I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have understood that correctly that a part of them were kept. But I cannot conclude from this report that those people who were kept were working up at the front line. That's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, and you are quite right. The second question is of a more general nature, and it has come up with another witness. If a commander says, "I want to take away 20 prisoners from Heliodrom," and the chief of Heliodrom knows or has strong reasons to suppose that these prisoners will be taken to do work on the front line, can the head of the prison refuse and say, "No, we will not release 20 prisoners for your purposes," full stop? Can he do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the warden or commander of the company for the POW shelter, if he is granted permission from the persons in authority to let them go, then he cannot refuse to let them go. But as from unauthorised persons, then he can, and then he will have to ask permission from the person in authority and authorised to do so at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a moment ago when I asked you questions about the governmental structure, it was to try and establish the circulation of information. Now, at your level, if at your level you were informed of this event, of things that happened, and you did nothing, how do the superior levels react if they depend on you? How can they act if they depend on you? So here we have a case where you have been informed that there are two persons who had escaped. Two persons were killed, and one person was wounded. That is a report that you received on an incident that was serious enough because it concerns the detainees, of course. Now, if you do not react to this at your level, how does the authority above you, superior to you, know what happened? Can you tell me, if you remember? The follow-up to this incident, what happened next, or don't you remember? And I can very well understand that in view of the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question that you've asked me, Your Honour. I cannot claim -- one cannot claim that there was no reaction, because the military police was working pursuant to the authority. Military police personnel are authorised persons, and whenever there is grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed they must act as professional in their line of duty, and it would be a sorry state if one would have to wait for an order from the minister for security. So there were reactions to these incidents, as there were reactions to all other incidents, and I'm sure that by the end of 1994 whenever detainees were missing an answer was found. And I do believe that my April order, when I wished to emphasise the duty to determine the responsibility of those people who acted towards prisoners and detainees outside or in violation of the Geneva Conventions be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please turn to document 7787, which is P 07787, please. Are you familiar with these documents, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what this document relates to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was compiled when I was absent from the HR HB, and from the office of the officer who replaced me, I can't remember who signed it, can't say who signed it, I can't understand the signature, but he received information. I assume it was information received from the SIS. He forwarded that to the defence minister and the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I'd like you to turn your attention to the document entitled, "Information report on the situation of the prisoner of war camp Heliodrom." Do you see that part of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what the subject matter of this information report is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's an error as far as the year is concerned in this report, or perhaps not. On the 1st of January a group of 60 prisoners was taken away by the commander of the defence for the town of Mostar, the 1st of January, 1994. And at the request of General Ante Roso, the prisoners were to be used for the needs of the defence of Mostar. They refer to the person who took them away. And reference is also made to the 13th of October, 1993, and to the fact that another group was taken away on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there, sir. The group -- let's focus on these groups one and a time. The group that was apparently taken out on 1 January 1994, when was that group returned?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of January, 1994, is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on -- on the length of time that these detainees were out performing labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was authorised by the chief of the Main Staff, and according to his authorisation they were out for 29 days. That concerns the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And now let's turn, sir, to the second group. When was the second group taken out?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And does the document indicate when those persons were returned?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of December -- on the 21st of December there was an exchange. Twenty prisoners were taken to the collection centre, and another 20 were taken charge of. And then it says that on the 22nd of September Mr. Ivan Andabak took charge of 20 prisoners. No written document accompanied this act. On the same evening he returned 13, but that means that seven were not returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see reference to any other group of persons being taken out for labour in this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of November reference is made to 59 prisoners who were taken out for the needs of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO. It refers to the person who took charge of the group. It also refers to the fact that on the 28th of January, 61 prisoners were returned, and it says that another 14 prisoners were missing, prisoners or detainees. And 16 were returned, but these 16 individuals were not from this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, with respect to these groups of unaccounted for or missing prisoners, do you have any information or did you receive any information as to what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time I can't remember, given that at the time I wasn't present down there for two months, but I believe that the military police administration did gather information on this matter. And I believe that Minister Jukic and Mr. Ante Roso also took certain steps after having received this report, but I'm not really familiar with this matter because I wasn't present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, sir, you told us -- or we saw a document and you explained to us how you were the person who could authorise prisoners to be taken out for labour. Can you comment or provide some general information as to what type of information you wanted or required in order to approve taking persons out to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there are any documents, but when I received such request I'd try to find out what the detainees were needed for and where they were needed, but I didn't receive such requests. The other thing I received was from the director of the Aluminijum plant, Mr. Brajkovic, and I knew him personally and I knew the purpose for which he would use such detainees, so I authorised this. I didn't authorise anything else. But the chief of the Main Staff also had the right to authorise such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, Mr. Biskic, when you make reference to the chief of the Main Staff, who are you referring to at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the chief of the Main Staff, General Ante Roso, because he issued an order, and in his order he also stated who could authorise such things, and he was one of the persons who could provide such authorisation. So we're referring to a period when he took over the duties as chief of the Main Staff, and in November 1993 he issued an order on banning people from being taken away to perform labour, and on the necessity of returning detainees to the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, what type of record-keeping requirements were in force with respect to requests or approvals to take persons out for labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, is sir, to document P 07878?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to another document, I'd like to dwell on what we have been dealing with. I'll take a few examples at random. The 19th of September, 1993, 50 prisoners were taken. On the 28th of January, 1994, 61 prisoners were brought in. My question is as follows: What kind of prisoners are you referring to here in your report? You remember the discussion we had awhile ago with regard to POWs and detainees. On legal terms, naturally, this poses a problem, but I want to know what category of prisoners we are referring to, according to your own definition. And the second subquestion is: Which ethnic group did these prisoners belong to, the prisoners who were brought in, taken out, and those who didn't return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in response to your first question, when we disbanded the collection centres we can talk about POWs [as interpreted] that we referred to. So on the 1st of January, 1994, those who were taken away were people who belonged to that category. They remained in the Heliodrom collection centre. When we're talking about the 17th of November, 1993, the group concerned is a group that hadn't yet been categorised, so I couldn't answer your question precisely. As to the nationality, their ethnic affiliation, I can't provide an answer to at that either. I believe most of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, just a clarification. He indicated war detainees, not POWs. I mean, it's in the translation. I believe it's on -- it's here someplace. I can't remember, but it's -- it's on -- it's on line -- line 8, page 46. It has "prisoners of war" when the gentleman indicated "war detainees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
