utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of that comment. With regard to this document, on the 3rd of February you forwarded a document to Mr. Jukic and to Mr. Roso. It concerned the situation that POWs in Heliodrom were in, and you added to your letter some information, a note, but what is more interesting is there is also a declaration concerning 61 prisoners that relate to certain events, and among other things they mention the fact that four prisoners had been killed by snipers, and three apparently had been killed by ABiH snipers, and one had apparently been killed by the HVO, someone called Roki. Someone who reads this document must take the situation into account and consider the conclusion reached in the information where you say that such methods must be prevented and punished, because it has obviously consequences to an international, political -- so you do your work. And my question is again as follows: Mr. Jukic, did he speak to you about this after the 3rd of February again or not? I'm putting this question to you because the -- if the subject appears important for the Judges, well, we can still call Mr. Jukic to testify before the Chamber if he is still alive. But having said that, did Mr. Jukic refer to the matter we're dealing with or not? Because you draft very alarming reports, and one expects results. So what did Mr. Jukic tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll repeat what I said when this report was sent. I was not in the area. I didn't sign it. An officer from my office signed it. And secondly, this information note and the statements supplied demonstrate that the matter was being dealt with. So SIS officials and members of the military police gathered information and did everything that was necessary in order to file a criminal report against certain individuals. What I can say is that the minister, Perica Jukic, was absolutely in favour of having conventions respected. He was against abuse of any kind and he was for measures to be taken. Whether he did anything else, whether he forwarded any information up the chain of command subsequently, I don't know. I can't say. But he was against such phenomena in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're saying on the 3rd of February you weren't in the area and that an officer signed on your behalf. Very well. Could you look at the B/C/S version because there is a handwritten reference, and I'm wondering whether you are the person who made this reference. Can you tell me whether this was your handwriting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Upon returning I had a look at the mail that had been sent by my officers, and it mentions prisoners of war -- rather, detainees, however you wish, that is what was referred to. So I was subsequently informed of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you returned, you a look at what had been written. You had a look at the statement, et cetera. You say that the minister of defence, Mr. Jukic, just like yourself, wanted international conventions to be respected. Very well. But did you discuss the matter with him, because what is referred to is not of a -- it's quite important. The International Red Cross was informed of this matter, and there was going to be a follow-up on an international level. So did Mr. Jukic talk to you about this problem or did you move on to other subject? That is what I would like to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, we spoke about how to deal with all the problems in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. We did not discuss this report in particular, but we discussed matters in general terms, and we did everything we could to make the system operational and to make sure that each and every element within the system functioned properly. I believe that the military police administration, the crime military police administration, filed criminal reports against those with regard to whom it was possible to prove that they had abused or maltreated POWs. As far as the report of the International Committee of the Red Cross is concerned, they had evidence on entry and exit from these locations. When I returned from the ministry of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, I asked from the chief of the military police, Colonel Siljeg at the time it, to tell me about what had been taken -- what steps had been taken as a result of their requests, and I wanted to know what results had been obtained by the military police with regard to the comments made by the International Red Cross with regard to the requests made by the International Red Cross. I want to point out that steps were taken, that we didn't fail to act, but given that 13 years have passed it's difficult for me to remember each and every detail, but on the whole we dealt with all the issues that are referred to here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to return briefly to the quality of the prisoners concerned, those taken to work. It seems that the information here comes from the ICRC people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the information we're discussing now is an information report that was drafted by the SIS, and there are letters from the International Committee of the Red Cross that have been added, and they discuss the same problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have a look at the beginning of the document that says, "Based on the report of the Red Cross in Medjugorje." Apparently the facts that have been mentioned are facts referred to given the information provided by the Red Cross. It's written here in black and white.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that this was an information that was compiled by the SIS, and on the basis of letters from the International Committee of the Red Cross. So they reacted to letters from the Red Cross. Whenever information was provided, steps were taken. There was a reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now, the ICRC is under the Geneva Conventions entitled to visit places where prisoners of war are detained, and I mean the war in its -- in its true meaning, and they have the right to talk to those prisoners. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: They do not have the right to visit any kind of prisoners unless there is a specific agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday or earlier on that since my arrival, and I believe that was the case before, too, the International Committee of the Red Cross could visit POWs whenever they wanted to do so, whenever they expressed this desire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now, if one looks at these two issues the report of the Red Cross on prisoners taken out to work and the comments of the Red Cross again, that would normally be and indication that the prisoners concerned were prisoners of war in the technical sense. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I don't quite understand the question, nor do I understand what I should agree with. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe it's a bit complicated. These informations on prisoners taken out to work in engagements which are not compatible with the Geneva Conventions come from the ICRC. The ICRC has competence exclusively to deal with prisoners of war. Must one not then assume that these prisoners were, in the technical sense of the term, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question now. However, in the area that we're discussing, the ICRC and the Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was responsible to deal with everyone who was in collection centres at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll conclude very rapidly, because I see that the Prosecution still has a lot of time, but I can't avoid putting this question to you: This document -- well, there's also a letter from Mr. Claudio Baranzini who was the head of the Red Cross in Medjugorje. It is addressed to you and the copy was from Mr. Pusic. It's dated the 10th of January and they say in this letter that they visited the Heliodrom, et cetera, and that a number of detainees referred to the issue of labour, and a number of HVO brigades, in particular the 2nd and the 4th Brigades had made these detainees work. So the Red Cross officially informed you of the problem. It's not without importance. It's an official letter that was sent to you. So my question is: Did you realise how important this letter was or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was aware of the importance of all the letters I received, and especially of all the letters I received from the ICRC, and all the letters that I received, regardless of the fact that they were also forwarded to other addresses, all these letters were sent to the military police administration so that they could check the allegations in the letters and so that they could respond to the ICRC and inform them of the results of the military police's investigation. So not a single letter from the ICRC at the time when I was responsible was ignored, and I believe that that was the case before too. I believe that not a single letter was ignored before my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, because apparently the Red Cross spoke to detainees, because when we have a look at the B/C/S document, and this can't be seen in the English translation, we can see that the famous statement regarding 61 detainees was handwritten, and it's been signed. We don't have 61 names, but we have 59 names, and each detainee signed. So the information that came to light was information that you should have paid attention to, and that is perhaps the reason for which you contacted your superior minister, your minister of defence. But didn't you think it would be useful to have a meeting with Mr. Baranzini?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that at the time I wasn't in the area, but as far as the representative of the Red Cross is concerned, the chief of the military police, Mr. Siljeg, had a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Mr. Siljeg had a meeting. Is he the person who was the HVO commander in Prozor before he was appointed as the chief of the military police? Can you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, before he was appointed as the chief of the police administration, was the commander of the Tomislavgrad military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We'll see whether this colonel should come to testify as a witness for the Chamber. Mr. Mundis, we'll discipline ourselves now and leave you sufficient time to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you turn now, please, to Exhibit P 07878, which again in your binder is marked 7878. Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with these documents that constitute P 07878?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me try this: Have you seen these documents before today?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I have. I do believe so, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The date of this document from Colonel Siljeg was during the time period you were back in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I do believe that I saw it after my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can we turn, please, to the page that has the subject line "List of people who were taken in 1993 and are currently on work sites"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just so that you are informed, Mr. Mundis, we have only the cover letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask then with the assistance of the usher that perhaps this document -- it should be available in e-court, but we can put it on the ELMO. Thank you for that, to avoid future problems here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, in the Croatian language the page that I'm referring to, subject line being "List of people who were taken in 1993 and are currently on work sites"? Do you see -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Biskic, what this document concerns in terms of the information that's being put forward?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a list of persons who were on work sites, and they were taken there in 1993. The document was compiled by the company commander for providing security to the POW shelter at Heliodrom. His name was Stanko Bozic, and he is addressing this to the chief of the military police, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, on the 2nd of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please -- can you please, sir, and perhaps if the -- if the document can be lifted up slightly on the ELMO so that we can see the bottom of the document. Let's just take, Mr. Biskic, the first cluster of this document under the heading "Convicts Battalion, Siroki Brijeg." Do you see that part of the document in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The "Convicts Battalion, Siroki Brijeg," that comes first. Is that the part you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is precisely the part, sir. Can you just briefly explain to the Trial Chamber the information that's contained under that heading so that we can understand how this report is structured?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says that: "Pursuant to the order from the coordinator in the president's office, Mr. Tomo Sakota, on the 1st of December, 1993, Robert Medic took away 20 people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, do you know who Robert Medic is or was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. The name doesn't ring a bell at all. I assume he was someone from the Convicts Battalion because it refers to the Convicts Battalion, or I assume it does, which had its headquarters in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us this position that Mr. Sakota had, coordinator, in the president's office? If you're familiar with what Mr. Sakota did as coordinator in the president's office, if you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if perhaps we can go on the English version to the next page, please. And if we could go a little bit up or down on the document. Now, Mr. Biskic, in the Croatian version you'll find under a stamp a sentence that starts: "At the request of Marinko Sosa." Do you see that in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We see an indication there, "... with the approval of General Petkovic ..."

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, earlier today, sir, you told us that there were a number of people authorised to approve the taking out of persons for labour. Is General Petkovic one of the persons so authorised, pursuant General Roso's order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you look at the date, it precedes the arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 23rd of October, 1993, and if we recall that a moment ago -- or, rather, in the course of the day we saw an order from General Milivoj Petkovic issuing an order that nobody without permission from the Main Staff could do anything, which means that General Milivoj Petkovic was the person who was in the capacity to give permission for detainees to be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn now, sir, to a different subject. That document can be removed from the ELMO. Earlier -- or just a few moments ago, Mr. Biskic, we were talking about documents you'd received from the ICRC. During the time period that you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you have a general idea as to the number of letters or other correspondence that you received from the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, about 10 at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Biskic, if letters were received from the International Committee of the Red Cross during the time period when you were back in Zagreb in early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, sir, what subject matters was the International Committee of the Red Cross raising in the correspondence that you received?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it mostly referred to the non-return of those who were taken out from the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to document 7537. That's P 07537. Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with this document? Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the letter from the ICRC dated the 10th of January. And a moment ago we had the letter when we discussed the information centre onto Minister Jukic on the 3rd of February [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to the next document, P 07636. And again, Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I received it before my departure for Zagreb, and if not then, then later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, do you have any knowledge or recollection as to how these letters from the ICRC were actually delivered to you or came to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the manner in which or, rather, when they arrived by post or fax? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for certain whether it was by fax or by post. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn -- let's turn our attention to this document, 7636. Do you have any recollection, sir, about receiving this letter in terms -- or that relates to the death of several prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this was the only such letter dealing with the death of detainees that you received from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again with respect to this document, P 07636, do you recall any specific steps that were taken to determine whether the information in this letter was accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in response from the chief of the administration of the military police that I asked for upon my return from Zagreb that there must be a response to this answer from the ICRC of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question is: Do you have any independent recollection of any steps that were taken?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of an investigation or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the sense of an investigation or a subsequent report that you might have received from anyone concerning the information set forth in that letter.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember just now. If there is a report, document, then we can see in it the results, whether what the ICRC was asking for here was complied with and whether steps were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to the next document, 8050, which is P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this document, this letter from the Red Cross, is addressed to you, and a copy was sent out to three people, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Pogarcic. Now, when I asked you a question about the structure of the government a moment ago, I was not aware of this document. Now, noting that we have three names here that appear, I'm going to ask you whether when you received this letter and you knew that a copy was sent to the Prime Minister and to his chef de cabinet or who was acting as chef de cabinet, did you not at that point in time report to your superior, the defence minister, and tell him you received a letter from the Red Cross which highlights a number of events? And then the Prime Minister also received a copy, so did Mr. Petkovic, and, "What are we going to do?" So do you remember that? Can you give us an answer? Because you can see that these were all high-ranking individuals to whom copies were addressed to. And so when I said a moment ago that the Red Cross brought up a subject, it had implications, and here is one of them because the Red Cross is sending copies to the head of the government. So what did you do at your level since it was you to whom the letter was addressed to? The others were just sent a copy by information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try and answer your question in the following way: First of all, after having received a letter like this I didn't have to ask my superior what I should do, because it was normal that I ask the military police to investigate all the allegations made in this letter, and that in keeping with its authority to undertake the necessary measures. And I believe that the minister, Mr. Jukic, was informed of this, but I had no -- I didn't have a separate reason, any special reason to ask him what I should do, because it was clear to me what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is this: At your level you received a letter from the Red Cross. You did what was necessary, which was to contact the military police about it, but you did nothing other than that, even if it was the head of the government that was one of the recipients of a copy of the letter, as was Mr. Petkovic, but still you did nothing more than that, just to ask the military police to look into the matter and see what had happened, that was all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday and today we have been discussing what was done to find people who entered collection centres and left them but where we have no records of that. We issued a number of orders, and I insisted and went to see Minister Jukic and said that he and others should take steps to supply us with information and that these people should be returned. And all this happened up until April when we realised that despite all the steps we had taken not everybody was returned. Then concrete orders were issued once again emphasising that an investigation should be conducted and a criminal conducted for individuals which were suspected of having mistreated the war -- the prisoners of war at any point. So this was something we insisted upon all the time. I don't have the individual results here nor can I remember what they were, but I am quite convinced that the military police records must have records of what steps were taken against somebody who was thought to have abused any prisoners of war in any way whatsoever, because one of the things I did was to solve problems like this in addition to the other tasks I had as deputy security minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have taken note of what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please turn to document P 08050. 8050. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw it upon my return from Zagreb at the end of March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what steps were taken to identify or locate the 365 detainees that are referred to in this document of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that the report from the chief of police of the military police contains that. And when I returned, I would be able to see what steps were taken with respect to this letter from the ICRC. And I'd like you to find that report, and I'm sure it will help us provide a response to that question in more concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to document 7796, P 07796. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we discussed this document a moment ago, earlier on, if it is 7796, because it's a document sent from my office to Minister Jukic and Mr. Roso, and we discussed it earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You're correct. This is the same as 7787, so we'll move on, sir, to the next document, which is 7895. P 07895. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw it upon my return from Zagreb, just like I said for the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, do you have any independent recollection of any steps that were taken with respect to the 76 detainees that are mentioned in the second paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but let me emphasise that the report from the military police should contain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Turn, please, sir, to document P 08014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. A short question on this document, 7895. The ICRC is making an analysis of Article 23 of the Convention and the legal aspects of it. That is to say that no prisoners of war should be detained in zones where they can be subject to combat fire. We know all about that. Now, the Red Cross is also talking to you about an agreement signed on the 22nd of May, 1992, in Geneva, and from the conference in London on the 27th of August, by which the ICRC should be informed of all persons captured and detained. Perhaps you ignored -- you didn't know about these international agreements on the 22nd of August and the other one. Now, when you received this letter, and you also see that Mr. Prlic was sent a copy of it, what were you going to do? Would you go to the foreign affairs minister to see what these agreements meant, or would you contact the ICRC, which in a previous letter had asked you for a meeting? What would have you done? What did you do on the 18th of February -- or, rather, the 19th of February, because apparently this letter was recorded on the 19th of February. So, what did you do on the 19th, as of the 19th of February to resolve this issue, which takes on now a number aspects, international aspects, the aspects of government, humanitarian aspects. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you asked me what I did on that day. If that is so, then on that day I wasn't there. I wasn't in the area. But pursuant to this document, we did what was done with the previous one. The military police investigated and the orders were repeated that those who had been taken out of the POW shelter Heliodrom should be returned. So these order are being repeated. And I said that the HVO units under the chief of the Main Staff -- were under the chief of the Main Staff and that he issued an order for their return. And we insisted upon this all the time. Some results -- we came up with some results, but at the end of the April we repeated the order from the military defence. We received an answer from the commander and continued our investigations into each and every person missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There, too, we have taken note of what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may for one second. The gentleman has indicated today and yesterday that irrespective of the classification, at least when he was there, that he wanted the Red Cross to have access to everyone, and I think that was his testimony. So in the overall context, I think his answer should also be taken into consideration with previous answers and I must say that at least -- the gentleman seems to be -- or at least some of the questions may give the gentleman the impression that he's being tried over here - I know that's not the intention - or that he's being treated as a suspect when he has never treated as a suspect, was not questioned as a suspect. So I think that in all fairness we should keep in consideration previous answers that the gentleman has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel has just told us that yesterday you said the Red Cross could have access to detainees. You told us that on several occasions. Very well. But when the Red Cross writes a letter like this where apparently they're having difficulties, what did you do faced with the situation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me repeat what I've already said, and I said that the International Red Cross Committee should come to the premises and facility where detainees were held and who were under the authority of the sector of which I was in charge. The detainees who were outside that facility or the POW shelter, I and the services subordinated to me exerted pressure on all those to have them returned so that they could be under our supervision and so that the ICRC could have access to them. That's what I said earlier on, and that's what I stress again, that those people who were taken out were not accessible to me either at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One clarification on the record, Your Honour, just on page 64, line 21. The gentleman indicated that they could have access, not that they -- or that could come, not that they should come. That's just a translation error or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, to answer another an element of the Defence counsel's intervention, when I put my question to you it wasn't a matter of suspecting you of anything. We just wanted to know what you would have done. You said the military police carry out an investigation. Defence counsel believes that you are a suspect of some kind. I asked you, you received a letter and what did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe that he is. I'm saying that the questions may give the gentleman the impression. Please. I mean, I don't want to turn the gentleman into a hostile witness against me. I never said that he is a suspect. I'm saying that the questions that are coming at the gentleman would give the appearance that he didn't act, first of all, and it seems to me that if anybody did act there, it was this gentleman here. But I don't want to give the impression that I'm suggesting that he's a suspect, but he may get that impression. So again I apologise, but I want to make sure the record is clear that the gentleman didn't think I'm being hostile to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't consider myself to be an accused. I know what I did. I know how I acted, and I'm proud of the way that I acted, given the situation I was in and given what it was possible for me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And again for the record, Mr. Biskic was never interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor as a suspect, and in fact, that point was specifically raised with him when we interviewed him, and he was specifically informed that he was not being interviewed as a suspect by this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, could you please now turn to P 08014. 8014 in your binder. And again, is sir, is this a document that you've seen before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Biskic, being made aware, other than from this letter, about persons being detained in the military police station in Gornji Vakuf or Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, about any steps taken to verify or determine whether this information in this letter was accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat. I believe that was the case, but I don't know who did this at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, is sir, to the next document, P 08031. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It dates from a period when I was in Zagreb. I believe that when I returned I saw it or was made familiar with it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, any steps that were taken to locate or find any information concerning these persons listed as being missing in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I believe that in the course of 1994, every person was probably answered for. I didn't receive answers for everyone when I was down there, but I believe that the investigations continued and that attempts were made to establish the truth for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to the next document in the binder, P 08026. Do you recall, Mr. Biskic, having seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 7th of April, 1994. I believe that I saw it when I returned. I believe it was one of the documents in the bundle of documents waiting for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And please turn to the following document, 8034, P 08034. Same question, sir. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be the same as the answer I gave you for the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The following document, sir, P 08036. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 8th of March, 1994. As far as I can see, the document wasn't forwarded to me, so I can't really claim that I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this with respect to this document, sir. Did you at any point in time while you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina become aware of citizens of German or Serbian nationality being detained?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any Germans, but as far as Serbs are concerned, well, yes, naturally there were detainees of Serbian nationality because war was being waged against the Serbs too. But I can't remember whether there were any when I arrived, because I didn't really look into the ethnic affiliation of the detainees. But as far as Germans are concern, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next document, sir, P 08079. Do you recall, Mr. Biskic, seeing this document upon your return from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that I did see this document when I returned from Zagreb. The date is the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn, sir, to the next document, P 08089. Same question, Mr. Biskic. Do you recall seeing this document upon your return from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as the answer I gave you for the previous one. I believe I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any independent recollection about individuals such as the seven prisoners listed on this document being detained in Prozor as of this time period?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember anything right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This might be an appropriate point for the next recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break, then you'll have an hour and 10 minutes, and it would be good if you could conclude within the hour and 10 minutes that you still have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I'd ask you now, sir, to turn, please, to P 08124, 8124. Sir, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter. I have the English version, so I need a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have the Croatian language version perhaps underneath?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MEG 94/111, is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, that appears to be signed by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed a document that I added to it and forwarded this to the chief of the military police, and MEG 94/111 is a document from the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Biskic, I'd just like to focus your attention on your letter, which is the covering letter to the ICRC document MEG 94/111. Can you read, sir, in the Croatian version of your letter the date that you sent this letter or the date of this letter, your covering letter?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't really see it well, but I think it's the 28th of March, 1994, I assume. That's when I returned from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the purpose of you sending this letter to the head of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I sent the letter regardless of the fact that he received this letter directly. I said what should be done so that the list would correspond to the records on the detainees in Dretelj, where the evidence on those exchanged by the office for exchanges and to carry out a conversation with the head of Dretelj at the time. It was also to inform the Red Cross and to launch a search for those who were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Biskic, on the 28th of March, 1994, do you recall who was the head of Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one, because at the time Dretelj didn't exist as a collection centre. This concerns the 15th of September, 1994. On the 28th of March, 1994, Dretelj wasn't operating as a collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn then finally, sir, to document 8070, P 08070.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Mundis. I would like to have an answer to -- to what really your question is. Who, Mr. Biskic, was this warden of Dretelj that you ordered to be talked to? You say, "Have talks with warden of KRZ Dretelj." Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have anything in particular in mind, but I assume that when Dretelj was in existence as a collection centre it had someone at its head, but I don't know who that person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, this document, P 08070, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it last time you provided me with it when we had a discussion. It wasn't forwarded to me or addressed to me, so I assume at that time I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There appears to be in this document a listing of a number of ICRC letters. Do you see that in this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you able, sir, to draw any conclusions based upon this listing of ICRC letters concerning Muslim detainees and the transfer of Muslim persons?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to read through the document, because I didn't draft it, sir. I can't really answer your question precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, of the fact that Mr. Pusic was receiving letters from the ICRC in the first few months of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could draw that conclusion on the basis of the letters that were addressed to me, too, and Berislav Pusic was referred to as one of the addressees. It's only on that basis that I could draw such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, in response to a number of questions asked both yesterday and today, you indicated a general awareness of the Geneva Conventions. Can you tell us, sir, what type of training or education you learned about the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of my education at the military academy for the land forces in Belgrade, I think I had a subject entitled military law, and when we studied the subject, we also studied international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions. And as an officer of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, we studied the Geneva Conventions, and we also educated member of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, and we implemented these rules and regulations in the course of our operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, about the standard training that professional officers coming from the JNA would have had with respect to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, we had to pass an examine on military law. To prepare for that examine we had to study those conventions and international humanitarian law as well. I don't believe we had any practical training sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately how many hours or days of instruction you would have had at the military academy in Belgrade concerning humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, during the time period that you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at any point in time did you attend any meetings where Dr. Prlic was present?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the -- there were three or four meetings, and the president of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Jadranko Prlic, was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the time period where you were at these three or four meetings where Dr. Prlic was present?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first meeting was two or three days after our arrival in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I think it was on the 13th of November, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the discussion was that Mr. Jukic informed the Prime Minister of the situation, of your arrival. I think Minister Jukic was present. I think it was a meeting that was held in his office. There was General Roso. I was there, and I believe that General Bobetko also attended the meeting, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the other meeting or meetings that you had that Dr. Prlic attended, do you recall approximately when the next such meeting was and what the subject of discussion was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the next meeting was held when we were implementing the decision of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on disbanding collection centres. I think it was a meeting held in the office of the Prime Minister, but I can't be sure. I think Mr. Berislav Pusic was with me. I think Mr. Pogarcic was there. And on the whole, I remember one sentence in particular according to which all activities should be coordinated with the ICRC. That's what the Prime Minister said. And as far as disbanding centres and the transfer of the detainees to third countries is concerned, and as far as moving across the front line to territory under the ABiH is concerned, I think that was also discussed. I can't remember the exact date, but I think it was between the 11th and the 15th, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of which month, sir? Which month?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: December 1993. That's the second meeting I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these two meetings, Mr. Biskic, do you recall any other meetings that you attended in which Dr. Prlic was present?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a meeting held perhaps on Christmas or just before Christmas, the 24th or 25th, but I think it was before the 24th, and it was held with Minister Jukic. I think that the Prime Minister informed us of initiatives that had been taken for a cease-fire. A cease-fire had been requested, a cease-fire with the ABiH for the holiday period, but apparently the ABiH had refused to agree to this. And as far as the international forces in the area are concerned, they wanted them to insist that by a certain date in January a cease-fire or, rather, a truce should be established, and we were expecting a truce with the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you make a comparison with respect to the status or quality of the military police forces of the HVO at the time you left Bosnia and Herzegovina in the spring of 1994 as compared with the situation as you found it when you arrived on 8 November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to make a comparison without being subjective. All I'd say is that when I left, all the units that were to be established were established. The chain of command was absolutely transparent. The military police was in charge, and as far as daily command is concerned, military police units were under the command of the HVO, under the command of a battalion of the military police in the military district, and, yes, they were under the command of the military district commander. As far as the system of information is concerned, it became fully operational and daily reports and information was compiled on other activities of the military police. There were few objections to the work carried out. The military police was no longer at the front line, because towards the end of December 1993 we managed to withdraw from the front line, and that was certainly perhaps the cause of the fact that the military police had not carried out its work as well as it could have before. No one objected to my work, so I believe that the situation that we left was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Retired Brigadier Biskic, I'd like to thank you for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. You completed your examination-in-chief within the exact time fixed by the Chamber, which means that we have 50 minutes left. Who is going to start off on the Defence side? Mr. Praljak's on his feet. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'm the first one. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Biskic.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm not a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we ask the usher's assistance to hand round the documents, please. I apologise. My microphone wasn't on, but may I ask the assistance of the usher to distribute the documents, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's just clear this matter up. The Croatian army, would you agree with me there that the Croatian army adopted the nomenclature of NATO ranks according to which brigadier was in fact brigadier general and is a one-star general. Therefore, you are a general, Mr. Biskic, and that's how I'm going to address you. Let's move on straight away to the beginning. When -- you came down there with a team numbering several persons and all of them were born on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe so, yes, although I didn't establish where each of the people were born, but I assume that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All right. So when you got there, did you come across any obstruction in your work?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, let me repeat. There were no obstructions to my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just give me a yes or no answer - in this case it is no - because I have very little time, and we have to get through a great deal of things.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: Did you while you were working in the Croatian army and in the HVO, from any of your superiors at any level, by some guidelines or instructions you were given, did you receive anything like that ever which -- or, rather, receive an assignment to conceal something bad that happened and was detrimental to the image that the army had?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever issue an order of that kind to anybody subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: According to what you know in the Croatian and in the HVO during the time that you served there, and the SIS and the military police, and the HVO, did they report about any evil deeds that happened exactly, whether it be killing, wounding, looting, or whatever, and whether or not the perpetrators were found or not, but was the reporting and information given correct and exact without anything being hidden?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, before your arrival on the territory of Herceg-Bosna, did you know that sometime in the second half of October long-lasting and forceful military operation by the BH army was completed? It was called Neretva 93. And the object of that operation was to reach the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards Croatia, that means.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you yourself spoke about this. Was it clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the question you have just asked is a question that was not raised in the main interpretation. You can ask such questions but not as leading questions, and you have been leading there. You must distinguish those two kinds of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely -- absolutely not, Your Honour. Absolutely not. That is not the rules. It is cross-examination. Now, if he's going beyond the scope of direct examination, if it's relevant, he should be entitled to do so. If it's not relevant, he should be cut off immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not saying he's not allowed to do so. I'm saying he should not lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I vehemently object to that. The rules for cross-examination is that there are leading questions and there is nothing in the rules that prevent this, nothing. This is something for the first time I hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I have not invented it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know you haven't invented it but it probably comes from some other system. But not in this system. So with all due respect, Your Honour, I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It comes from an American source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No it does not come from -- well, I'd like to see the American. I'll correct him right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Can I assist on that, Your Honour. I think what Your Honour has in mind is that in -- in certain common law jurisdictions there is a rule that if you want to go beyond the scope of direct examination you may have to bring the witness back as a witness for your own side of the case, and in that case, of course, you wouldn't be allowed to put leading questions in that form of examination, and sometimes there are -- if you call an opposing party or witness identifying an opposing party that could also be the case but, Your Honour, that rule has not been adopted in the Tribunal, and I think under Rule 90(H) Mr. Karnavas is right because if the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case of the cross-examining party, then he may cross-examine about the subject matter, and indeed there's no restriction in the Rule on leading questions. So I think Your Honour may have had that particular common law rule in mind, but, Your Honour, it doesn't appear to be reproduced in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in the Tribunal. So in my respectful submission, Mr. Praljak's question would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, continue your questioning, but as my colleague said, in order to reinforce your thesis, it would be advisable that the witness himself tells us what you want him to say rather than you guiding and leading the witness. But it's up to you to see how you're going to obtain a result, how you're going to score. Continue, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will remain by the question and its precision, because the man came as an assistant for security. That post cannot be taken on without knowing the previous situation. That's the first point. Number two, the witness said quite clearly that straight away upon his arrival he worked with operative knowledge, operational knowledge, in order to conduct a military operation in Uskoplje and thus lessen the pressure from the BH army in Central Bosnia. I think that was sufficient reason for me to ask the question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, is it clear to you that the commander of the HVO, which was me at the time, had every right to ask the chief of the military police to place at his disposal all the available manpower so that I would be able to defend the territory that was under jeopardy? Is that clear to you, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to something that is called republican citizenship. When in the former Yugoslavia you filled out various forms providing personal data, was there a column which said "citizenship," and then you would write SFRY, or "nationality," SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You wrote "Croat," did you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But then there was a column which said "Republican citizenship," and in the republican citizenship column all of us born on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina would write "BiH"; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you, too, were a citizen, the republican citizen, of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in April 1992, I became a citizen of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you did not ask them to strike you from the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you'll agree that I didn't ask for that either. I didn't ask to be struck off that register either.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know that General Roso was a citizen of France, for example?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that because he was a member of the Legion d'honneur, and I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the foreign legion, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about Mr. Cepic? Was he a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about Minister Susak? Was he a citizen of Canada, a Canadian national, in view of the fact that he had emigrated after having been persecuted, and he emigrated to Canada a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he lived in Canada, and I assume he had Canadian citizenship too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about General Crnjac? Was he born in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Right. Fine. And the others, I don't want to enumerate them all. But anyway, all the people I mentioned, including me, in that legal vacuum with the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia, we found ourselves in a position - would you agree with me there? - whereby we joined up with the Croatian army, but we did not cease to be responsible to the citizen -- to citizenship of BH. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know, and I showed the Trial Chamber a document, that during 1991 and 1992 there were cases of the kind that I have mentioned now in the Croatian army, and they numbered about 14.000 people who were actually born in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, but I am quite convinced and assume that there were that many. Anyway, there were a great many. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when on the 15th of January, 1992, in Croatia a sort of truce was signed, or towards the end of the year anyway, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina preparations were being made for the war that would break out in 1992, a large number of these people felt the need to defend their own homes in the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at that time was within the composition of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, and I said in the previous discussions that I wanted to leave at the beginning of the war to Posavina; however, because of my duties in the Ministry of Defence I was not given permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Because your extended family lived in Posavina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: May I have document 3D 00443 next, please. It's a document dated the 8th of April, 1992, signed by the deputy chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army for the combat sector, General Petar Stipetic. Do you know who General Stipetic is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was he a general in the Yugoslav People's Army as well before he moved to join the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 3D 00443 is the number of the document I'd like to be shown on e-court. Do we have the document in no. It's in the bundle. You have the document in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is problem with e-court we have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document I have is the one shown me by the Prosecution. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll show you the right document in a moment. Mr. Biskic, take a look at that document. And from this we can clearly see the position of the Croatian army vis-a-vis this problem. That is to say that people fought as volunteers in an army of a state, and now their homes were being attacked in the place where they were born. And let's focus on paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, General Praljak. Your Honour, either I need the English version on the ELMO or I need a copy of the bundle, because we don't have ... THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we move on? I apologise, Mr. Mundis, for not placing the English version before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It says "People cannot have the HV patches or any other HV documents." Is that a clear order?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It says all types of material aid can be given as well as professional assistance in the organisation of defence and other forms of resistance, and so on and so forth. Is that order clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, move on to the next document, 3D 00300. Here we have another clear instruction from the defence minister to all the Croatian army units signed by the minister of defence, Mr. Gojko Susak, on the 7th of July, and it says that, "Not a single officer, commander, is allowed to send or deploy the Croatian army outside the borders of the Republic of Croatia. Anybody who does so without receiving express orders from the Supreme Commander" - and do we agree that Dr. Franjo Tudjman was the Supreme Commander? - "he will bear all the consequences of his actions. If volunteers from the Croatian units who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina wish to go to the battlefield and defend their homes, the commanders must not prevent them from doing so." Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now, may we go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that I was the assistant or, rather, the deputy minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia for information and propaganda activities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have a document of mine dated the 31st of August, 1992. This document also concerns the exact instructions as to how members of the Croatian army can be taken to the battlefield in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It says: "We suggest that you avoid taking repressive measures," and then this says: "Given the fact that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a foreign state," is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does this show clearly that in the political department of the Ministry of Defence the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a foreign state was never in dispute, and this was the case significantly prior to the commencement of the conflict? Based on the fact that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a foreign state, and this was made public on television by the minister of defence, et cetera, et cetera, is that what it states here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's now move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered the question, but it's not in the transcript because it wasn't quite clear. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once more. Does this sentence show that the political section of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and I was in charge of it at the time, never doubted the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a foreign state?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case, and that was quite clear to me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let's have a look at the following document: 3D 00313. General Biskic -- not Blaskic. We all have Blaskic on our mind to a certain extent. I do apologise. General Biskic, you are aware that in the Republic of Croatia there were training centres where members of the ABiH were trained. You were a member of the military police force? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To an extent that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have a look at this here. We have a list of certain locations, Zagreb Borongaj, Zagreb Sljeme, Jastrebarsko, Pljesivica, Kutina-Zutica, Sisak-Zazina, et cetera. As a member of the military police were you aware of centres where members of the ABiH were trained in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were being provided with assistance when it came to training and equipment, but I wasn't aware of the locations of these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's have a look at the following document: 3D 00314. 3D 00314. The establishment of the units of the ABiH in the territory of the Republic of Croatia in 1992. Were you aware of the fact that in the territory of the Republic of Croatia the 77th Brigade was established as well as the Berbir brigade, the 17th Brigade, and the Handzar Brigade, and all of these brigades after they had been established joined the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about some of these brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which ones were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in Rijeka, I think. I can't remember this name, but I do know it was in existence. I'm almost familiar with the name Handzar and Berbir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the following document 3D 00299, 3D 00299. You have the document before you. Could you show us the heading. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the office of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. The letter was addressed to the Ministry of Defence Zagreb, and the date is the 4th of January, 1993, and the text signed by Colonel Hasan Efendic, have you ever heard of Colonel Hasan Efendic who was a military representative later on?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: He says further needs of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina allow HV officers to be engaged as follows: Avdic, Ismet; Ahmet Puskar; Dr. Rakanovic, Sadik, Colonel. Judging by their surnames are these people Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the surnames, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It states the status of these officers should be dealt with as has been the case to date, and I emphasise the fact, as has been the case to date. They should have all the privileges that HV officers should have, and having carried out their task it should be made possible for them to continue operating through the HV. Is that what it says here, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does this word, "responsibilities," mean? Does it mean what you had when you were in the HVO? You have your salary in the Republic of Croatia, but when you return you return to your previous position is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a number of people from the Croatian army and on the same principles they went to the ABiH more of them went to the ABiH than the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean did more of them join? I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When we see that there were these brigades and when we examine all the documents on assistance provided to the -- Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Republic of Croatia and we have a hundred thousand such documents at our disposal. According to the information you have, did more members of the Croatian army go to the ABiH than to the HVO on the basis of the same principle?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the answer would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at the following document -- let's have a look at 3D 00795. 3D 00795. This is a document we received from the office for national security from the Croatian intelligence service. The subject is assistance to the Ministry of the Interior when it comes to establishing an establishment system for the armed forces of the republic of Herzegovina in 1992. Are you familiar with the name Brzovic, Ivan, who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tomislav Druzak, do you know this name, the name of the head of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The document is a lengthy one. There are many names in it. It says, "In the course of 1992 and 1993," this is the third paragraph, "on several occasions equipment was sent to the most jeopardised areas and major cities in a systematic and organised way and it was picked up in Zagreb by authorised individuals from the HVO and the BiH Territorial Defence such as" and then there are certain names that follow. It says the places to which equipment was sent are as follows and then you have a list of names. Given the names, can you see that there are more Muslims who came to collect equipment than there were Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Given the place names, the names of the places that the equipment was sent to, can you see that there were more places that were under the control of the ABiH than places under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll just read out another section. In the course of the early war years in Bis, the role of the logistics and communication section changed and certain humanitarian and economic sectors were also covered, and then after the beginning of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH they ceased using the system by the HVO while the ABiH continued to use other methods of cryptographic protection. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next document. My --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the question. The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that we tried to help the establishment of the term in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in all way. We assisted displaced persons, refugees of Muslim nationality, my -- believe that among other things this area that's referred to here was also covered. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at 3D 00794. 3D 00794. That's a document dated the 3rd of October, 1995, and it concerns the establishment of Porobic's brigade. In the second paragraph it says the brigade was active from April to August. For some time they were involved in combat in the Derventa area and briefly in Central Bosnia in the area of Hadzici or, rather, Pazarici. While staying in Hadzici, the brigade had about 600 men, and about 150 returned to Rijeka. The fate of the others is not known. Does this show that these 150 men that returned to Rijeka returned to the Croatian army after their work in the ABiH had come to an end?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the conclusion that could be drawn from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Mustafa Porobic retired, do you know that Mr. Mustafa Porobic was a retired officer of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps before we move on to the next document, could we kind some kind of indication as to the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is clear from the header of the document. I mean, it was disclosed to the Defence upon the request of the Defence from the official body of the Republic of Croatia, but the author is obvious from the header. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We have another series of authentic documents on this brigade; unfortunately, I have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, we have discussed knowledge of the Geneva Conventions and of military law. Do you know that I, as the deputy minister for political activities in 1992, immediately after my appointment, together with the ICRC launched an initiative to educate Croatian soldiers and -- with regard to the Geneva Conventions and war law?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did we on that occasion issue tens of thousands of booklets that were distributed to soldiers, booklets that dealt with what was permissible in law and what wasn't permissible?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case. In the Croatian army there were many such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At all levels --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
